transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-31
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya N. (Redwood SE), Alex (Solutions Architect), Evan M. (CISO), Priya K. (Head Cloud), Marcus L. (Security Architect), Lina D. (Compliance)

Summary:
Short: Deep dive on Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture. Main focuses: SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO and SCIM/SAML mapping, audit logs and retention, KMS/CMEK/HSM options, network isolation (ingress/egress), firewalling model, peering/VPN, and PoC next steps.

Topics:
- SOC 2 / ISO documentation and pen test summaries
- Network isolation patterns: VPC, private subnets, NAT, egress filtering
- Firewalling: security groups, NACLs, managed firewall appliances, and host-level controls
- Ingress: ALB/NLB, customer-managed bastion or private LB, mutual TLS options
- Egress controls: proxy vs NAT gateway, allow-lists and CIDR restrictions
- KMS and encryption: CMEK, bring-your-own-KMS, HSM requirements and key rotation
- Audit logs: CloudTrail-like capture, SIEM integration, log retention policies
- RBAC/SSO: SAML, Okta SCIM provisioning, mapping groups to Redwood roles

Action items are recorded separately below.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey team, thanks for carving time on the 31st, uh, appreciate it. Today we're focused on the Private VPC security architecture for Sentinel Finance, specifically the netsec and compliance controls, so we'll try to cover ingress/egress, firewalling, and how we integrate with your KMS and audit pipeline.
[00:12] Evan: Great, yeah thanks Jordan. We've got some tight constraints — EU data residency for some products, and our compliance team needs to see how logs are retained and who can access keys.
[00:20] Priya K.: Also want to understand traffic flows for egress since we have a managed firewall and DLP appliance — we need to know which IPs to allow.
[00:30] Jordan: Yep, totally. Priya N., Alex will dig into the architecture. Priya?
[00:33] Priya N.: Thanks. So first a quick overview: Redwood Private runs a customer-dedicated control plane that can be placed in your VPC or in an air-gapped on-prem cluster. For VPC mode we provision customer subnets for control plane components and we recommend separating the inference runtime nodes into private subnets with no public IPs.
[00:50] Marcus: Quick Q — when you say control plane, is that still managed by Redwood or do we host it entirely? We need to be clear on network boundaries.
[01:00] Priya N.: Good question. We have two patterns: 1) Hosted control plane with customer-managed data plane in your VPC (we run control plane in Redwood but it talks over a private peering or mTLS connection), or 2) fully private where control plane components are also deployed into a customer VPC or on-prem — in that mode the control plane APIs only exist inside your network. For Sentinel, given regulatory needs, we recommended fully private so nothing traverses public internet.
[01:23] Evan: That sounds preferable, can you explain the ingress model? How do we get traffic in for inference requests?
[01:30] Alex: Yeah — for ingress we typically front with an internal NLB (Network Load Balancer) or a private ALB depending on L7 requirements. The recommendation for low latency is NLB with TLS termination at the host or mutual TLS at the client side if you need strong auth. If customers require a single egress point we can route through a proxy cluster.
[01:55] Lina: Do you support mTLS with client certs issued by our PKI? We have internal CAs.
[02:00] Priya N.: Yes, mutual TLS is supported. We can integrate with your PKI; you provide certs or a signing authority, we configure the runtime to validate client certs. For private control plane we can do mTLS edge-to-edge.
[02:12] Marcus: About firewalling — we run Palo Alto between subnets, so we'd prefer predictable ports and CIDR ranges. How stable are your port requirements?
[02:22] Priya N.: We keep a small set: control plane API ports (443/8443), runtime gRPC ports (typically ephemeral but we can pin ranges), SSH only to bastion (22) if you allow, and internal health/metrics ports. We'll provide a port/CIDR matrix. For gRPC we can pin external-facing ports to a range to satisfy firewall rules.
[02:40] Evan: What about egress? Our security policy forbids wide internet egress from private subnets.
[02:45] Jordan: Right — Redwood supports egress via customer-managed NAT or proxy. We can configure the runtime to only call specific endpoints (e.g., for OS package updates or model downloads) and prefer using an internal artifact mirror so you can block external egress entirely after initial setup.
[03:03] Priya K.: And for model artifacts, can they stay in your private S3/Blob or must they come from Redwood's repo?
[03:10] Priya N.: For Private we support pulling model artifacts from your storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) via VPC endpoints or peered buckets. We also support registry replication — we can replicate images to your repo during the PoC so no external calls.
[03:22] Marcus: Ok, good. On the KMS side: we require CMEK with keys in our HSM and strict key rotation — does Redwood support BYOK and our HSM provider?
[03:32] Alex: Short answer: yes. We support CMEK and integrating with customer KMS for encryption at rest. For cloud providers we integrate with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and GCP KMS. For HSMs and FIPS requirements we support customer-managed HSM via KMIP or cloud HSMs — the exact integration varies, but we can do a bring-your-own-key flow and configure the runtime to never persist unencrypted keys.
[03:55] Lina: (brief) Are there audit trails showing which Redwood user rotated keys or accessed KMS?
[04:00] Priya N.: We emit audit events for key usage—who requested a key operation from the Redwood control plane — and those can be forwarded to your SIEM. For HSM-backed keys, the cloud provider's KMS/CloudHSM logs also contain usage events, which we recommend forwarding to your central logging.
[04:14] Evan: On logs: retention is critical. We need logs for 7 years for some products. How does Redwood handle long-term retention and log export?
[04:22] Jordan: We don't store long-term customer logs in our managed service unless it's a paid add-on. For Private deployments you can configure local retention policies and forward all audit, access, and system logs to your SIEM e.g., Splunk, Sumo, or GCP Pub/Sub. We support direct CloudTrail-style exports, syslog, and S3-based archives.
[04:40] Marcus: Do you mask PII in logs or is that on our side?
[04:44] Priya N.: By default we avoid logging raw customer content. Application-level payloads are not stored in audit logs. We log metadata — request IDs, user IDs, model/version, token counts, latency. If you need additional redaction we can add a scrubber in the pipeline before logs are forwarded.
[04:59] Evan: Good. On RBAC and SSO: we use Okta and need SCIM provisioning, role mappings, and fine-grained roles — can Redwood map Okta groups to RBAC roles and support attribute-based access?
[05:12] Alex: Yes — Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (admin, operator, observer, auditor). For attribute-based policies we can integrate with an external policy engine or accept group attributes for role resolution.
[05:29] Lina: Do audit logs show user-level actions aligned to Okta identities?
[05:33] Priya N.: Yes — with SCIM/SAML mapping, user IDs in audit logs match your SSO identities. We recommend enabling SCIM so user lifecycle is synced and we capture the federated identity.
[05:43] Marcus: For network policies inside the cluster, do you rely on security groups only or do you support host-based firewalls and iptables hardening as well?
[05:50] Priya N.: We recommend defense-in-depth: security groups/NACLs as the first line, then iptables/host firewall and process isolation at the runtime. We also support sidecar proxies for mTLS enforcement between services.
[06:05] Jordan: Another question from our compliance checklist — pen testing and vulnerability management. How do we share your CVE patch cadence and results?
[06:12] Priya N.: We publish a patch and CVE bulletin. For Private customers we can provide a copy of the internal vulnerability management policy and recent scan summaries. We also offer an option for a joint pen test if required.
[06:24] Evan: About data residency: we need to ensure EU workloads never leave the EU. Does the Private VPC model guarantee that?
[06:30] Alex: If you deploy the entire stack in an EU region and keep model artifacts and logs in EU-local storage, nothing will leave. We provide region pinning for deployments and can ensure model image registries are local. For any external services (like optional telemetry) we can disable or route to EU endpoints.
[06:48] Priya K.: On network peering — we use both transit gateway and a hardware VPN for some DR paths. Will Redwood work with transit gateway peering and static routes?
[06:56] Priya N.: Yes — we support peering to TGWs, VPNs, and direct connect. We'll need route tables and allowed CIDRs to configure expected flows. We can also support static routes for on-prem connectivity.
[07:10] Marcus: How do you handle software updates for runtime nodes? We want patching done in maintenance windows and avoid auto pulling images from public repos.
[07:18] Alex: For Private deployments we provide a controlled upgrade process: we push images to your repo, coordinate a maintenance window, and use rolling upgrades. You control when to apply patches.
[07:27] Evan: Incident response — what level of access do you need to troubleshoot if an incident happens?
[07:33] Jordan: Typically for Private we ask for temporary access via your bastion or a support VPN with scoped roles, and we do it under a formal support engagement. All actions are audited and logged.
[07:45] Lina: Are these support sessions recorded in the audit logs?
[07:48] Priya N.: Yes, every support action is logged and linked to the operator identity. We can provide a support session playbook and required approvals.
[07:58] Evan: Anything special about container runtime security? Do you support gVisor or other sandboxes?
[08:05] Priya N.: We support container hardening, seccomp, and can run pods under restricted profiles. For extra isolation we can integrate with sandbox runtimes — there's an operational cost but it's doable for high-security environments.
[08:18] Marcus: Back to egress filtering and firewalling — we have a DLP that requires egress to go through a proxy. Does Redwood support HTTP proxy env vars and mTLS to an outbound proxy?
[08:27] Alex: Yes — the runtime supports outbound HTTP/S proxy and we can configure mTLS to the proxy if needed. For non-HTTP outbound we recommend using a NAT gateway behind your firewall appliance.
[08:38] Evan: On the audit logs format — do you provide structured JSON logs or plaintext? Our SIEM wants JSON with specific fields.
[08:45] Priya N.: We emit structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, request_id, user_id, action, resource, model, version, latency_ms, node_id. We can extend the schema if you need additional fields.
[08:57] Lina: For long-term retention, we might want to push logs to an immutable S3 bucket with WORM. Is that supported?
[09:03] Priya N.: Yes — you can configure the log sink to write to S3 with lifecycle rules and WORM/Compliance mode enabled. We support S3, GCS, Azure Blob.
[09:12] Marcus: What about database encryption for metadata?
[09:16] Alex: Metadata stores use encryption at rest by default. For Private you can provide a CMEK so the DB is encrypted with your key.
[09:22] Evan: Ok. Any limitations on keys per region or KMS calls per second?
[09:27] Priya N.: KMS quota is typically driven by the provider. We batch operations where possible and cache decrypted secrets in memory for short durations. We'll model expected KMS QPS in the PoC.
[09:38] Jordan: Let's cover the network diagram at a high level — Priya, can you walk through the reference?
[09:43] Priya N.: Sure. High-level: public management subnet (optional) -> bastion or private management jumpbox -> control plane subnets (APIs, management) -> internal runtime subnets (GPU nodes) -> private NLB for inference ingress -> egress through NAT/proxy -> peering to customer networks. Firewalling: security groups on each layer, NACLs for subnet-level control, and optional perimeter firewall (Palo Alto) in front of NAT. Logging: flow logs to your logging VPC or S3.
[10:11] Marcus: For flow logs, do you recommend VPC Flow Logs or an agent on the nodes?
[10:15] Alex: VPC Flow Logs are good for network-level telemetry; for application payloads we recommend a sidecar or agent that emits richer metadata. Both can be forwarded to SIEM.
[10:25] Evan: For the PoC, we want minimal open egress and full log export. Can you replicate that?
[10:29] Jordan: Absolutely. That's the typical PoC config. We'll lock down egress to only allow your SIEM endpoint and artifact repo, replicate images into your registry, and forward logs immediately.
[10:37] Priya K.: Regarding authentication to the runtime API, how's token management handled?
[10:41] Priya N.: We support short-lived tokens issued by the control plane, or API keys for programmatic access. For enterprise, we recommend OIDC tokens backed by your IdP, with RBAC enforced server-side.
[10:52] Marcus: Can we scope tokens to specific models or routes?
[10:55] Alex: Yes — tokens can be scoped to projects, models, or roles. We provide fine-grained route permissions.
[11:03] Evan: Any specific compliance certifications you can share now?
[11:06] Jordan: We can share our SOC 2 Type II report, ISO27001 certificate, and our pen test summary. We'll send redacted artifacts per legal.
[11:13] Lina: About log access — who at Redwood can see customer logs?
[11:17] Priya N.: By default, Redwood engineers do not have access to customer logs in Private deployments unless granted for support. Access requires approval and is fully audited.
[11:27] Marcus: For on-prem, how do licensing and updates work?
[11:30] Alex: On-prem is licensed and we push binary updates that you apply. We provide patch notes and a recommend window.
[11:37] Evan: Great. Anything else we should note for the compliance team?
[11:41] Lina: A few items: ensure we get MOU on support access, minimum audit retention and confirmation of where keys live. Also need SLA around incident response and an escalation list.
[11:52] Jordan: We'll include those in the engagement doc.
[11:55] Priya N.: One more technical note on egress and model updates: some model loaders contact remote registries for telemetry; we can disable telemetry and ensure all downloads are from your repo.
[12:06] Marcus: Ok, feels good. About performance impact of host-level firewalls and sidecars — any numbers?
[12:12] Alex: Sidecars add small latency depending on model size and batch size; for typical token generation we see <5% overhead with optimized proxies. We'll run benchmarks in the PoC.
[12:22] Evan: Let's sync on next steps then.
[12:25] Jordan: Action items already captured: Jordan will send compliance artifacts, Priya will share architecture diagram and port/CIDR matrix, Marcus will send CIDR and peering details, Lina will share retention requirements. We'll set up PoC kickoff w/c 2027-01-10 pending your availability.
[12:38] Evan: Thanks everyone.
[12:40] Priya K.: Thanks.
[12:41] Jordan: Thanks, happy new year early.

End of transcript.
